title: A framework to evaluate the performance of Variational Quantum Algorithms
abstract_summary: The paper introduces a general framework to benchmark variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) for QUBO problems by combining three metrics—feasibility, quality and reproducibility—and visualizing trade-offs via a normalized quality diagram. Reproducibility is formalized using Shannon entropy and a decision criterion under resource constraints is proposed; the approach is demonstrated in simulation on a 16-qubit QUBO using CVaR-based cost functions and varying shot counts.
methodology_description: The authors propose a statistical framework to evaluate Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) on QUBO problems by interpreting parameterized quantum circuits as distributions over bitstrings and mapping per-run outcomes to points (ncalls, pmin) in a normalized two-dimensional "quality diagram." They define three complementary metrics computed from the empirical distribution of outcomes: feasibility F (probability that pmin ≥ pthreshold), quality Q (expectation of a quality function q that zeroes below pthreshold and otherwise measures a weighted Euclidean distance to the ideal point), and reproducibility R (1 minus normalized Shannon entropy of the empirical distribution discretized on a 0.1×0.1 grid). As a proof of concept the authors run simulated experiments on a single random 16-qubit QUBO instance: they use the RealAmplitudes ansatz (reverse-linear entanglement, one repetition, 32 parameters), COBYLA as classical optimizer and CVaR-based cost functions with α ∈ {0.15,0.25,0.50,0.75,1.00}. They sweep measurement shot counts s ∈ {1000,5000,10000,20000,30000,40000,60000,80000,100000} and perform n = 400 independent optimizations per VQA configuration (initial circuit held fixed). Statistical estimation uses binomial/CLT for feasibility (confidence intervals at 95%), sample mean and standard error for Q, and asymptotically normal entropy estimators with variance via the delta method for R. Decision thresholds used for selection are F0 = 0.70, Q0 = 1.20 and R0 = 0.60; outputs include tabulated F, Q, R with 95% CIs, quality-diagram visualizations and a final set of VQA configurations meeting all thresholds.
experimental_setup: Simulation (no physical QPU). Single random QUBO instance of dimension N = 16; RealAmplitudes ansatz (reverse-linear entanglement, 1 repetition), COBYLA optimizer; multiple CVaR cost functions and shot counts were swept; 400 independent runs per VQA configuration; results reported with 95% confidence intervals.
experiment_input: Random QUBO instance (symmetric Q ∈ R^{16×16}) used for all experiments; problem instance and the randomly chosen initial quantum circuit are stated to be available upon request. No preprocessing reported beyond standard QUBO formulation; problem size corresponds to N = 16 binary variables / qubits.
experiment_process: For each VQA configuration (ansatz + CVaR α + shot count s): 1) initialize the ansatz parameters to the same randomly chosen initial circuit for all runs; 2) run COBYLA to optimize the chosen CVaR(α) cost estimated from s measurement shots; 3) record per-run ncalls (number of circuit evaluations during optimization) and pmin (probability of sampling a global minimum by the final circuit); 4) repeat steps 1–3 for n = 400 independent optimizations to obtain an empirical VQA distribution over the quality diagram; 5) compute feasibility F as the fraction of runs with pmin ≥ pthreshold, compute quality Q as the empirical mean of the q(ncalls,pmin) quality function (which zeros below pthreshold and otherwise uses a weighted Euclidean distance to the ideal point), compute reproducibility R = 1 − S/Smax where S is Shannon entropy of the discretized distribution (grid 0.1×0.1, K=100); 6) compute 95% confidence intervals (binomial/CLT for F, sample-mean SE for Q, asymptotic entropy variance via delta method for R); 7) apply selection thresholds F0, Q0, R0 to choose best configurations.
experiment_output: Tabulated metrics per VQA configuration: feasibility F, quality Q, reproducibility R, each reported with 95% confidence intervals; quality-diagram visualizations (scatter/contour of ncalls vs 1−pmin and level curves of q); selection list of VQA configurations that meet thresholds (F0=0.70, Q0=1.20, R0=0.60). No external algorithmic baselines (classical solvers) are reported.

[speculative] Reproducibility of VQA runs can be meaningfully quantified by the Shannon entropy of the distribution of outcomes on the quality diagram, normalized to produce a reproducibility score in [0,1].

[speculative] A decision/selection procedure based on thresholds (F0, Q0, R0) on feasibility, quality and reproducibility can be used to classify whether a VQA is a suitable solver under resource constraints.

[supported] The framework was exercised in simulation on a single 16-qubit random QUBO instance using a RealAmplitudes ansatz (one repetition, reverse-linear entanglement), CVaR-based cost functions for α ∈ {0.15,0.25,0.50,0.75,1.00}, COBYLA optimizer, shot counts s ∈ {1k,5k,10k,20k,30k,40k,60k,80k,100k}, and n=400 independent optimization runs per VQA instance.

[supported] Empirical simulation results show that feasibility (probability of achieving p_min ≥ p_threshold) increases with both CVaR parameter α and number of shots s and tends to saturate as s grows (saturation observed around ~20k shots in these experiments).

[supported] Empirical simulation results show that the proposed quality metric also generally increases with α and s, with evidence of saturation beyond ~20k shots for most α values (exception noted around α = 0.25).

results_summary: The paper proposes a theoretical framework to evaluate VQAs for QUBO problems via three metrics—feasibility, quality, reproducibility—and a quality diagram representation. The framework was demonstrated in simulation on a 16-qubit random QUBO using CVaR objectives across a range of α and shot counts, with 400 runs per configuration. Simulation results show that higher CVaR α and larger numbers of shots generally improve feasibility and quality, with performance saturating around ≈20k shots in these tests. Reproducibility (measured via Shannon entropy) was largely insensitive to shot count. Using preset thresholds, the authors identified a set of VQA configurations (higher α and large s) as best-suited for the tested instance. The work is presented as a benchmarking methodology; no claims of empirical quantum advantage are made, and the authors note limitations and the need for broader validation including hardware experiments.
performance_claims: Feasibility example: for α = 1.00 and s = 100,000 the measured feasibility was 0.95 ± 0.03 (95% confidence interval).
Quality example: for α = 1.00 and s = 60,000 the measured quality was 1.40 ± 0.04 (95% confidence interval).
Reproducibility example: for α = 0.15 and s = 1,000 the reproducibility score was 0.69 ± 0.02 (95% confidence interval).
Observed saturation: feasibility and quality metrics show diminishing improvement beyond ~20,000 shots for most α values in these experiments.

Selection outcome: with thresholds F0=0.70, Q0=1.20, R0=0.60 the VQA configurations selected as well-suited were {(α=0.75, s=10k),(0.75,30k),(0.75,60k),(0.75,80k),(0.75,100k),(1.00,60k),(1.00,80k),(1.00,100k)}.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — Proposes a practical, statistically grounded framework to benchmark VQAs on NISQ-era hardware constraints by sweeping shot counts and reporting feasibility, quality and reproducibility with confidence intervals.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Treats parameterized quantum circuits as probabilistic samplers and evaluates hybrid runs where a classical optimizer (COBYLA) tunes circuit parameters; framework explicitly captures per-run optimizer behaviour (ncalls) and sampling success (pmin).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Introduces a "quality diagram" (normalized ncalls vs 1-pmin) and formalizes reproducibility as 1 minus normalized Shannon entropy of the empirical distribution over the diagram, enabling visual trade-offs between feasibility, quality and reproducibility.
#limitation:simulation-only — All experiments are performed in classical simulation on a single random 16-qubit QUBO instance; no experiments on physical QPUs are reported.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — The framework is demonstrated on one synthetic QUBO instance with no comparisons to classical solvers or to alternative quantum/hybrid methods, limiting claims about real-world performance or advantage.
#limitation:qubit-count — Demonstration is limited to N=16 qubits (single small QUBO), which constrains conclusions about scalability to practically relevant problem sizes.
